item.title: Goldman says hedge funds pile into shorts, with ETF shorts posting a 19-point weekly jump
item.description:
Low hedge fund positioning cuts both ways. It limits the pool of forced sellers if the selloff resumes, but it also means a stabilization in prices could trigger short covering and re-risking that lifts stocks faster than fundamentals alone would suggest. The steady $150 billion of retail and retirement inflows provides a floor under large-cap indices, especially the mega-cap names those funds hold most. Homebuilders and other consumer-cyclical stocks with crowded shorts could be the most volatile if sentiment turns. With US markets closed for Thanksgiving, any re-risking is unlikely to show up until next week.

---

Professional investors are hedged and waiting for prices to stabilize, while retirement savers keep buying, and that split could shape how the next rally unfolds.

Summary:

  • Goldman's Vincent Lin says hedge funds cut exposure for five straight weeks, then added short positions in stocks, index futures and ETFs
  • ETF shorts rose about 19 percentage points in a week, the third-largest weekly increase in a decade
  • Clients rotated toward staples, utilities and REITs, favored hyperscalers within tech and shorted homebuilders
  • Hedge fund and trend-following positioning is near multi-year lows, while ETF and mutual funds took in about $150 billion in a month
  • Fundamental long-short funds were up about 7% this year, down from about 17% at midyear
  • Lin still favors hyperscalers and healthcare over consumer staples, and is watching tech earnings, payrolls, CPI and the Fed

Hedge funds have moved from cutting risk to actively betting against the market, according to Goldman Sachs, a sign of how fragile sentiment has become during this month's selloff in technology stocks.

Vincent Lin, co-head of Prime Insights and Analytics in Goldman's FICC and Equities business, said on the bank's The Markets podcast that hedge fund clients reduced their exposure for five straight weeks. Last week the selling stopped, but clients turned more defensive by adding short positions in individual stocks and in index futures and ETFs. ETF short positions rose by about 19 percentage points in a single week, the third-largest weekly increase in the past decade. The episode was recorded on November 23, before Wednesday's US inflation data.

Where the money is moving

The rotation has favored defensive sectors. Consumer staples, utilities and real estate investment trusts have clearly outperformed over the past month, helped by lower volatility, less reliance on consumer spending and little connection to the AI trade. Within technology, clients have preferred the biggest cloud and AI platform companies, known as hyperscalers, for their stronger balance sheets and steadier earnings. On the short side, they have targeted economically sensitive consumer areas, especially housing and homebuilders, where positioning has fallen to multi-year lows.

Fast money retreats, slow money keeps buying

Lin drew a sharp contrast between types of investors. Hedge funds and trend-following funds are near the bottom of their historical positioning ranges, and retail day traders have pulled back. But slower-moving retirement and mutual fund investors remain heavily invested, with ETF and mutual fund products taking in about $150 billion over the past month even as markets fell.

That gap matters for the near-term outlook. Lin said that when uncertainty is high, buyers tend to wait for higher prices before stepping back in. Hedge fund managers want to see prices stabilize before adding risk, and with the year nearly over, many are focused on protecting gains rather than chasing a rally. His models point to more supportive flows if prices steady or start trending higher.

Why hedge funds are cautious

Lin pointed to two drivers. The first is performance. Fundamental long-short equity funds were up about 17% at midyear but only about 7% at the time of recording, which he characterized as a setback rather than a collapse. The second is the AI story itself. Lin said "the best of the AI infrastructure returns is probably behind us," and that the trade is shifting toward how companies make money from AI, a transition he noted has historically been the hardest phase of major technology cycles.

He remains constructive on parts of the market. Lin still favors the hyperscalers and argues they should be relative winners if computing capacity stays tight, adding that any slowdown in AI spending could free up cash for buybacks. He also prefers healthcare over consumer staples, citing more attractive valuations and earnings drivers less tied to AI.

What to watch

Lin flagged late-season tech earnings, US payrolls next week and November inflation data in about three weeks as the key tests, along with whether the Federal Reserve's hawkish stance holds. Since the recording, hotter-than-expected core PCE inflation has kept a December hike firmly priced. That leaves the near-term backdrop little changed for cautious hedge funds.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: The RBA's three 'stars' are fuzzier than they look: what it means for AUD and stocks
item.description:
The article doesn't signal any change in policy, but it supports the RBA's data-dependent approach, and that has practical consequences for traders. When the central bank can't be confident where neutral sits, the market's estimate of the peak cash rate is likely to stay unsettled, which tends to mean larger swings in short-term Australian bond yields and the Australian dollar around major data. The same debate is playing out at the Federal Reserve and the Bank of Japan, so uncertainty over neutral rates is a global source of volatility in rate expectations, not just a local one.

---

Earlier:

  • Australia's data centre boom drives the biggest capex jump in years, near mining-boom highs

---

The RBA has admitted, in some detail, that it can't see its guiding stars clearly, which is exactly why traders should watch the data the central bank is watching.

Summary:

  • An article in the RBA's November Bulletin examines the uncertainty around three "star" variables: the NAIRU, potential output and the neutral interest rate
  • It finds that the usual measure of uncertainty, the range of estimates across models, captures only part of the true uncertainty
  • The neutral rate is the most uncertain, with model estimates often spanning 2 to 3 percentage points
  • Estimates can be revised substantially, by as much as half a percentage point for the NAIRU, including for past periods
  • The broad direction can still be clear: the RBA's models gave only a very small chance that unemployment was above the NAIRU between 2023 and 2025
  • Research cited in the article suggests relying more on observed data when star variables are uncertain, which raises the market importance of each data release

Central banks steer interest rates partly by reference to benchmarks no one can see. A new article from the Reserve Bank of Australia explains just how uncertain those benchmarks are, and the answer matters for anyone trading the Australian dollar, bonds or local stocks.

The article, "Uncertainty About the Stars" by RBA economists Leon Berkelmans and Matthew Read, appears in the November edition of the RBA Bulletin, published on Thursday. Its central message is that the "star" variables policymakers use to judge how hot the economy is running are much harder to pin down than commonly used measures suggest, and that the neutral interest rate is the hardest of all.

What is the RBA Bulletin?

The Bulletin is one of the RBA's regular publications. It is released quarterly at 11:30am Sydney time (0030 GMT), with articles also published on an ad hoc basis, and it carries analysis of economic and financial developments as well as articles on the RBA's history and operations. This edition contains two articles, one on small business conditions and this one on star variables.

The Bulletin isn't a policy statement. The articles are written by RBA staff and reflect their research rather than a decision of the Monetary Policy Board. They are still worth reading, because they show how the bank thinks about the economy and which tools sit behind its decisions.

What are the "stars"?

The article covers three benchmarks, often written with a star symbol:

  • The NAIRU: the unemployment rate consistent with low and stable inflation. If unemployment falls below it, wage and price pressure tends to build.
  • Potential output: the level of GDP the economy can sustain without generating inflation. The gap between actual output and this level is the output gap.
  • The neutral interest rate: the inflation-adjusted cash rate that neither stimulates nor restrains the economy. A policy rate above neutral is restrictive, and one below it is stimulatory.

None can be observed directly. They must be estimated with economic models, so they come with error bands.

What the RBA found

The authors show that the usual shortcut for measuring uncertainty, the range of estimates across the RBA's suite of models, gives a misleading sense of precision. The RBA's six NAIRU models currently differ by only about 0.15 percentage points, yet the uncertainty band within the models spans about a full percentage point. Estimates also get revised as new data arrive, by as much as half a percentage point for the NAIRU, and those revisions often change the past as well as the present. The latest update raised the NAIRU estimate, but the authors stress that this was a reassessment of its level rather than a sign it had risen during the quarter.

The neutral rate is the most uncertain of the three. Estimates from different models have often spanned 2 to 3 percentage points, a range the authors describe as large compared with normal movements in the real cash rate.

There is an important reassurance. Uncertainty about the exact level of a benchmark doesn't always mean uncertainty about the direction of the economy. The RBA's models gave only a very small chance that unemployment was above the NAIRU between 2023 and 2025, meaning the labour market was clearly tight even if no one knew exactly how tight.

What it means for traders

The most important point for markets comes in the article's discussion of policy. It cites research suggesting that when star variables are highly uncertain, policymakers should put more weight on observed data such as inflation and changes in unemployment. Treating uncertain estimates as precise risks large policy mistakes.

For traders, that translates into three practical points:

  • Data releases carry more weight. With the cash rate at 4.85% after five hikes this year, the RBA can't say with confidence how far above neutral it is. That makes inflation, jobs and activity data the main guide to its next move, which tends to mean sharper moves in short-term yields and the Australian dollar on surprises.
  • The peak rate is a wide range. If the neutral rate could sit anywhere in a band several percentage points wide, so could the eventual peak in rates. Market pricing for the RBA's path can shift quickly, and the Australian dollar often moves with it, especially relative to the US dollar while the Federal Reserve is also raising rates.
  • Rate-sensitive stocks feel it first. Banks, property trusts and consumer stocks on the ASX tend to react most to changes in the expected path of rates, so data-driven repricing usually shows up there before it reaches the broader index.

Australia isn't alone. Bank of Japan staff put Japan's neutral rate somewhere between 1.1% and 2.5%, and that ambiguity has fed directly into yen volatility. The lesson travels well: when a central bank can't locate neutral, the market's best guide is the same data the central bank is watching.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BoJ's Tamura says rates must reach neutral 'soon', still sees neutral near 2%
item.description:
With a December hike already largely priced, the speech matters mainly for expectations of where the cycle ends. Tamura's 2% neutral estimate sits at the top of the market's assumed endpoint of 1.75% to 2%, so any sign that his view is spreading on the board would lift Japanese government bond yields at the short end and support the yen. Yen bears may test how much the BoJ is willing to do, with USD/JPY near 159 and intervention risk in the background. His explicit openness to accelerating hikes makes upcoming Tokyo CPI and wage data more sensitive for the yen.

Newswire cut: BoJ hawk Tamura says rates must reach neutral soon and still puts neutral near 2%, well above the 1.25% policy rate. He warns Japan's less firmly anchored inflation could require a faster pace of rate hikes if upside price pressures keep building.

One-line wrap: Tamura wants the BoJ to get to neutral soon and believes neutral is a long way above today's rate, which makes him the clearest voice on the board for a longer hiking cycle.

Summary:

  • BoJ board member Naoki Tamura said the policy rate should be brought to neutral "soon", and he still puts neutral at around 2%
  • He said financial conditions remain accommodative, with the 1.25% policy rate "still some way" from neutral
  • He described the approach as "make haste slowly" and said the BoJ could assess each hike's effects within a few months
  • Tamura said weaker anchoring of inflation expectations means the BoJ should respond faster to overshoots, including by speeding up hikes
  • He cited producer prices up 7.1% from a year earlier and CPI excluding temporary measures at around 3.5% as signs of upside risk
  • He said AI-related demand is boosting a much wider range of Japanese industries than he expected

Bank of Japan board member Naoki Tamura called on Thursday for interest rates to rise to a neutral level "soon". He repeated his view that neutral sits around 2% and warned that the central bank may need to speed up its hikes if inflation pressures build.

Tamura, one of the board's most hawkish members, was speaking to local leaders in Yamanashi at 0100 GMT (2000 US Eastern on Wednesday). His remarks reinforce expectations of a rate rise at the BoJ's December 17-18 meeting and suggest he wants further increases well into 2027.

Policy is still loose, and neutral is a long way off

The BoJ raised its short-term policy rate to around 1.25% in September. Tamura said financial conditions remain accommodative and the policy rate is "still some way" from neutral, the level that neither heats nor cools the economy. He said he first put neutral at around 2% in June and that his view hasn't changed.

That gap matters for markets. If Tamura is right, the BoJ would need roughly three more quarter-point hikes to reach neutral, more than many investors expect. He was candid that neutral can't be known in advance and can only be found by raising rates and watching how the economy responds. The point echoes the RBA's discussion of uncertainty around the neutral rate in its latest Bulletin.

Make haste slowly

Tamura described the right approach as "make haste slowly". He argued that the BoJ can judge the impact of each hike within a few months by talking to firms and reading surveys, and that a thorough assessment doesn't have to be a slow one. Most firms, he said, see the effect of past and near-term hikes on their business as limited, although some have started to warn that higher borrowing costs will restrain investment.

He also flagged the option of moving faster. Inflation expectations in Japan have only recently risen from very low levels, so Tamura said they are less firmly anchored than in the United States or Europe. In his view, that means the BoJ should respond more quickly and strongly to signs that inflation is overshooting, including by speeding up the pace of hikes.

Upside risks are building

Tamura laid out why he is worried about inflation running above the 2% target. Producer prices rose 7.1% from a year earlier in October, driven by high oil prices linked to the Middle East conflict, the weak yen and AI-related demand. Those costs are now reaching consumers. He said CPI inflation excluding temporary government measures has risen to around 3.5%, and pointed to sharp price increases in items such as plastic goods and laptops.

He was also struck by how far the AI boom reaches. He said it is helping a much wider range of Japanese industries than he expected, from data centres to power equipment, air conditioning and construction. He described Japan as rich in "pick-and-shovel" firms, the businesses that supply the tools for a boom rather than taking part in it directly, a reference to the suppliers who profited most from the California Gold Rush. He added that AI is likely to push prices up in the short term, even if it lowers them later through higher productivity.

What it means for the yen

Tamura's views are well known, so the speech is unlikely to shift December pricing much on its own. The more important signal is his push for a faster path toward 2%, which is at the top end of market pricing for an endpoint of around 1.75% to 2%. A more hawkish path would generally support the yen, which is trading near 159 per dollar, close to levels that have previously raised the risk of intervention by Japanese authorities. The weak yen is itself one of the inflation pressures Tamura cites, which makes his case for steady hikes harder to dismiss.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bank of Korea hikes to 3.25%, sees 4.1% growth in 2027 as chip boom drives economy
item.description:
With the hike fully priced, the won and Korean bonds are likely to react more to Governor Rhee's guidance than to the decision itself. A signal that one more hike is coming would support the won and push up short-term yields, while hints that the cycle is ending could ease pressure on rate-sensitive stocks. The 4.1% growth forecast for 2027 is a strong vote of confidence in chip demand, which may help steady Samsung and SK Hynix after this week's selloff, but it also ties Korea's rate path closely to the global AI spending cycle.

---

Earlier:

  • Nikkei and Kospi rebound over 1% as Asia follows Wall Street's comeback, BoK decision next

---

South Korea's central bank is raising rates into a chip boom, betting that growth above 4% can absorb tighter policy while inflation slowly returns to target.

Summary:

  • The Bank of Korea raised its base rate by 25 basis points to 3.25%, in line with a Reuters poll
  • It's the third hike since July, after a pause at 3% in October
  • The bank forecasts growth of 3.9% in 2026, 4.1% in 2027 and 3.0% in 2028
  • Inflation is projected at 2.7% in 2026, 2.4% in 2027 and 2.1% in 2028
  • A semiconductor export boom and rising Seoul home prices underpin the tightening
  • Markets now await Governor Rhee's guidance, with economists expecting one more hike to 3.50% in early 2027

The Bank of Korea raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 3.25% on Thursday, its third increase since July. A semiconductor-led export boom is keeping the economy growing strongly and inflation above target.

The decision, announced at around 0100 GMT (2000 US Eastern on Wednesday), matched expectations, with 32 of 34 economists in a Reuters poll forecasting the move. It follows back-to-back hikes in July and August and a pause at 3% in October, when the board kept its tightening bias.

New forecasts underline the strength

Alongside the decision, the central bank released updated projections that show an economy running well above its usual pace. It now expects growth of 3.9% this year and 4.1% in 2027, before easing to 3.0% in 2028. Inflation is forecast at 2.7% this year, slowing to 2.4% in 2027 and 2.1% in 2028, so it only gets close to the bank's 2% target by the end of the forecast period.

The inflation projections for this year and next are unchanged from the bank's August outlook, which suggests the board sees price pressures as sticky rather than worsening. Growth of more than 4% would be exceptional for South Korea, and it explains why the bank has room to keep tightening.

Chips drive the economy, and the hikes

Semiconductors sit at the centre of the story. South Korea's chip exports nearly quadrupled from a year earlier to a record in the first 20 days of November, and made up almost half of total exports. That boom has lifted incomes and investment, while home prices in Seoul have climbed sharply, adding to the central bank's concerns about financial stability.

What comes next

The focus now turns to Governor Rhee Chang-yong's guidance on whether this is the last move. Economists in the Reuters poll expected one final hike to 3.50% in early 2027, while some local surveys see the peak as high as 3.75%. Whether the board was unanimous, and whether its statement keeps language about further tightening, will shape that debate.

Market reaction has been limited so far. The Kospi was up about 1% in morning trade, recovering part of Wednesday's slide of more than 6%, as investors weighed the steady policy outlook against volatility in global chip stocks.

For markets, the risk lies in the gap between strong local fundamentals and fragile global sentiment. A chip-driven economy gives the Bank of Korea reason to keep rates higher for longer. But any reversal in global AI spending would hit the same exports that are powering growth, and could quickly change the outlook for rates. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Australia's data centre boom drives the biggest capex jump in years, near mining-boom highs
item.description:
The surprise is large, but the market reaction is likely to stay muted because so much of the spending is imported equipment that does little for local output or wages. Investors are more likely to focus on what it says about capacity pressure and the RBA's December decision, where any lift in hike odds would support the Australian dollar and push up short-term yields. The industry mix matters for equities: the boom is concentrated in data centres and technology rather than mining, which favours data centre operators, construction and electrical contractors, and power suppliers over the resources sector that dominated past investment cycles.

---

Australia's investment boom is back near mining-boom highs, but this time it's being built from server racks rather than iron ore mines.

Summary:

  • Private capex rose 12.2% in the September quarter, against a 4.4% forecast and a 3.6% fall in Q2, and was up 18.6% from a year earlier
  • Equipment, plant and machinery spending rose 23.1% to a record, while buildings and structures rose 1.7%
  • Investment in information media and telecommunications, which includes data centres, rose 86.7%, with equipment spending up 183.5%
  • Non-mining capex rose 16.0% against 1.4% for mining, and Victoria led the states with a 31.0% rise
  • Firms' fourth estimate of 2026-27 spending rose 11.8% to about A$224 billion, with equipment plans up 20.4%
  • Heavy reliance on imports will limit the GDP boost, and the RBA meets again on December 7-8

Australian business investment surged far beyond expectations in the third quarter. Private capital spending jumped 12.2% from the previous quarter, almost three times the 4.4% rise economists had forecast, Australian Bureau of Statistics data showed on Thursday.

The figures, released at 0030 GMT (1930 US Eastern on Wednesday), put total capex at about A$59.5 billion for the quarter in inflation-adjusted terms, 18.6% higher than a year earlier. That takes it close to the peak reached during the mining investment boom more than a decade ago.

The jump came almost entirely from equipment. Spending on plant and machinery soared 23.1% in the quarter and 34.3% from a year earlier, reversing an 8.9% fall in the June quarter and lifting it to a record. Investment in buildings and structures rose a more modest 1.7%.

The industry detail points clearly to data centres. Total investment in information media and telecommunications, the industry that includes data centres, rose 86.7% in the quarter, and its equipment spending nearly tripled, up 183.5%. Earlier this year the ABS attributed a 6.5% jump in March-quarter capex to data centre equipment such as server racks and processing gear, and the June-quarter fall was widely seen as payback. Mining investment rose just 1.4%, while non-mining capex climbed 16.0%. Victoria led the states with a 31.0% rise.

Firms also plan to keep spending. Their fourth estimate of capital expenditure for the 2026-27 financial year came in at about A$224 billion, 11.8% above the previous estimate. Planned equipment spending was revised up 20.4% to about A$102 billion, far outpacing a 5.6% upgrade for buildings and structures.

There is an important caveat. Much of that equipment is imported, so a large share of the spending flows offshore rather than adding to domestic output. The boost to Australia's GDP will therefore be considerably smaller than the headline suggests. The ABS also completed its annual seasonal review with this release, which caused minor revisions to the equipment series.

For the Reserve Bank of Australia, the data still adds to the case that the economy is running hot. The RBA raised its cash rate to 4.85% on November 3, its highest since 2008 and its fifth hike of the year, in a split 6-3 vote. The board said inflation remains broad-based and likely to stay above 3% for longer than previously expected, but it dropped its explicit warning about further increases.

The RBA's final meeting of the year concludes on December 8, with the decision due at 0330 GMT (2230 US Eastern on December 7). October inflation data and third-quarter GDP figures will carry more weight before then, but strong investment intentions make it harder for the board to argue that demand is cooling.

The figures also stand out against a global backdrop of growing resistance to data centre projects, from Tokyo's suburbs to Australia's own Northern Territory. In Australia's biggest cities, at least, the money is still being spent.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6655 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nikkei and Kospi rebound over 1% as Asia follows Wall Street's comeback, BoK decision next
item.description:
The early gains look more like relief after a heavy selloff than a new rally, so the Bank of Korea's guidance could quickly decide whether Seoul holds them. A hawkish signal on further hikes could firm the won but weigh on rate-sensitive Korean stocks. In Japan, the yen near 159 per dollar keeps intervention risk in view, and any hawkish comments from Tamura could lift the yen and trim exporter gains. Treasury yields edging higher in Asian trade are a reminder that the inflation backdrop hasn't changed, which limits how far the rebound can run without fresh support.

---

---

Asia is taking its cue from Wall Street's late recovery, but with New York shut for Thanksgiving and the Bank of Korea about to speak, the rebound has little to lean on.

Summary:

  • The Nikkei 225 rose about 1.3% to around 57,700 in early trade after falling almost 3% on Wednesday
  • The Kospi gained about 1.2% to around 4,750, and the Kosdaq rose more than 2%, after the Kospi's 6% slide on Wednesday
  • Wall Street recovered from steep early losses to close higher on Wednesday
  • S&P 500 futures rose about 0.3% and Nasdaq 100 futures about 0.1%
  • Mainland China and Hong Kong open later, after both fell on Wednesday
  • The Bank of Korea decision and a speech by BoJ board member Naoki Tamura are both due around 0100 GMT

Asian stocks opened higher on Thursday, recovering part of Wednesday's heavy losses after Wall Street staged a late comeback. Thin holiday trading and a Bank of Korea rate decision are likely to keep moves cautious.

Japan's Nikkei 225 rose about 1.3% in early trade to around 57,700, after falling almost 3% on Wednesday. South Korea's Kospi gained about 1.2% to around 4,750, and the tech-heavy Kosdaq climbed more than 2%. The rebound is modest next to Wednesday's slide, when the Kospi dropped more than 6% as chip stocks were hit hard.

The lead came from New York, where stocks recovered from steep early losses to close higher on Wednesday, with the Dow erasing a drop of more than 1,000 points. The early selling had followed hotter-than-expected US core PCE inflation and strong growth data, which kept a December Federal Reserve rate hike firmly priced. US stock index futures extended the gains in Asia, with S&P 500 futures up about 0.3% and Nasdaq 100 futures up about 0.1%.

Mainland China and Hong Kong markets open at 0130 GMT, after the Shanghai Composite fell about 2% and the Hang Seng about 1% on Wednesday.

The next test for Korean stocks comes at around 0100 GMT (2000 US Eastern on Wednesday), when the Bank of Korea announces its final policy decision of the year. Economists widely expect a quarter-point hike to 3.25%, so the bank's guidance on further tightening is likely to matter more than the move itself. Bank of Japan board member Naoki Tamura, one of the board's hawks, speaks at the same time, ahead of a December meeting where markets expect a hike.

Trading is likely to be lighter than usual. US stock and bond markets are closed for Thanksgiving and Friday is a shortened session, which leaves Asian investors without a fresh lead from New York for the rest of the week. Thin liquidity can exaggerate moves on any surprise headline, whether from Seoul, Tokyo or the Gulf, where this week's tanker attacks have kept Brent crude around $91 a barrel. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Citi says fear is extreme, but stocks rose after 13 of 14 past VIX spikes to 40
item.description:
Contrarian calls like this tend to gain traction when other big names lean the same way, and this week Bank of America and Michael Burry have both pointed to the correction as a chance to buy. That could support dip-buying in large-cap US stocks once full trading resumes after Thanksgiving. The weak point is that the signal relies on volatility and sentiment, while the risks markets are worried about, hot inflation, a Fed on a hiking path and stress in AI credit, are fundamental. A renewed rise in the VIX would test the thesis quickly. Korean chip stocks could get support from the export data Citi highlights.

--

Citi Wealth argues the market is more scared than the numbers justify, and history suggests that extreme fear has usually been a better time to buy than to sell.

Summary:

  • Citi Wealth says investors with excess cash should consider buying stocks, while fully invested investors should hold
  • Its S&P 500 sentiment indicator fell to -2.1 on November 20, well below the -1.25 level historically followed by above-average six-month returns
  • The VIX briefly hit about 40 the same day, its highest since April 2025, and the S&P 500 rose three and six months later in 13 of the previous 14 such cases
  • Citi points to strong earnings and broad capital spending, with 48% of S&P 500 companies raising capex by more than 10%
  • South Korea's chip exports nearly quadrupled from a year earlier in the first 20 days of November, which Citi cites as evidence of strong AI demand
  • The view depends on earnings continuing to grow

Citigroup's wealth management arm says the fear gripping stock markets has gone too far, given what is happening to the economy and corporate earnings. In a note on Wednesday, Citi Wealth said investors with excess cash should consider putting it into stocks, while those already fully invested should stay the course.

The call rests on a sharp contrast. Citi Wealth's S&P 500 sentiment indicator, which tracks market volatility and trading activity, fell to -2.1 on November 20. That's well below the -1.25 level that has historically been followed by above-average returns over the next six months. The gauge also showed unusually high fear in October.

The VIX, Wall Street's best-known measure of expected volatility, briefly hit about 40 the same day, its highest since the April 2025 tariff selloff. Citi notes that in 13 of the previous 14 times the VIX reached 40, the S&P 500 was higher three and six months later.

Meanwhile, the fundamentals Citi watches have held up. The bank still sees corporate earnings as strong. Business investment is also broad: in May, 48% of S&P 500 companies raised capital spending by more than 10% from a year earlier, compared with a historical median of about 40%, and the increases weren't limited to big tech. Citi also describes AI demand as strong despite the recent drop in chip stocks. It points to South Korea's semiconductor exports, which nearly quadrupled from a year earlier to a record of roughly $38.5 billion in the first 20 days of November.

Citi adds that declines of 10% or more are relatively unusual when corporate earnings aren't shrinking. The S&P 500 has already fallen more than 11% from its October record.

The argument has limits. The VIX record covers only 14 cases, which shows a historical tendency rather than a promise. More importantly, the case depends on earnings continuing to grow. That leaves it exposed to the risks driving this month's selloff: inflation that is still running hot, a Federal Reserve on a hiking path and growing stress in the debt markets that fund the AI build-out.

Citi isn't alone in seeing an opportunity. Bank of America this week called the correction a better entry point, and Michael Burry has closed his bearish bets on the Nasdaq-100. For investors, the practical message is to treat extreme fear as a reason to review cash levels rather than a signal to sell, while watching earnings for the first sign that the fundamentals are turning.

item.title: Projectile explodes near tanker 50 nautical miles off Dubai as Gulf shipping attacks mount
item.description:
Incidents without damage rarely move oil much on their own, but where this one happened matters for pricing. An attack near the UAE coast, inside the Gulf, puts loading routes that had looked relatively safe back in the risk picture, which tends to show up first in war-risk insurance premiums and tanker freight rates rather than in headline crude prices. Asian refiners, the biggest buyers of Gulf crude, are the most exposed to any further disruption. With US markets shut for Thanksgiving and liquidity thin, a more serious incident could cause an exaggerated price move before the full market returns.

No one was hurt and nothing was damaged, but a blast near a tanker off Dubai shows that the threat to Gulf oil shipping is no longer confined to the Strait of Hormuz.

Summary:

  • A tanker reported an explosion from an unknown projectile close to the vessel about 50 nautical miles west of Dubai at 2130 GMT on Wednesday, UKMTO said
  • The crew are safe, with no damage or environmental impact reported, and authorities are investigating
  • Attacks on shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz are at their highest since the Iran war began in late February
  • Iran said this week that several tankers hit naval mines in and east of the strait
  • Oil flows through Hormuz are running at about half of pre-war levels, according to Kpler data
  • Brent traded around $91 late on Wednesday, still well below its wartime peak

A tanker reported an explosion from an unknown projectile close to the vessel about 50 nautical miles west of Dubai late on Wednesday, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency said. It's the latest in a run of attacks on shipping that has kept Gulf oil supply under pressure.

The incident happened at 2130 GMT on November 25 (1630 US Eastern). The ship's master reported that the crew were safe and accounted for, with no damage to the tanker and no environmental impact. UKMTO, which monitors commercial shipping in the region, advised vessels to transit with caution while authorities investigate. It didn't identify the tanker or say who fired the projectile.

Background: a waterway at war

The Strait of Hormuz, the narrow channel between Iran and Oman, normally carries a large share of the world's seaborne oil. Since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in late February, Tehran has tried to close the strait, and the United States has imposed a blockade on Iranian ports. The International Maritime Organization has confirmed more than 130 incidents involving commercial vessels in the Gulf, the strait and the Gulf of Oman since the war began.

Recent developments: attacks at a new high

November has been especially busy. Reported attacks in and around the strait have reached their highest level since the conflict began, according to maritime data cited by CNN, as Tehran tries to reassert control while oil prices fall. This week, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said three tankers hit naval mines and caught fire in the strait despite a US escort, and Iran's navy said another tanker struck a mine east of the strait on Wednesday. On Sunday, UKMTO reported a tanker involved in an incident with military forces in the Gulf of Oman.

Wednesday's incident stands out for its location. It took place inside the Gulf, well west of the strait and close to the UAE coast, echoing earlier November attacks on tankers off Qatar and Saudi Arabia. That suggests the risk is spread across Gulf shipping lanes rather than confined to the chokepoint itself.

Supply focus: flowing, but well below normal

Oil is still moving, but at reduced levels. Shipping data from Kpler put oil flows through Hormuz at about half of pre-war levels as of November 24, and shipments through the strait fell in the first half of November as attacks increased. US-escorted transits have helped keep some traffic moving. Iran has also reportedly allowed vessels linked to Iraq, Qatar, China and India to pass, which suggests it is managing who uses the strait rather than shutting it completely.

That partial recovery explains why prices have eased in recent weeks despite the violence. Brent crude was trading around $91 a barrel late on Wednesday, up more than 2% on the day, but still well below its wartime peak.

The risk for the oil market is that each new incident, especially further inside the Gulf, raises insurance and freight costs and could deter shipowners who have only recently returned. For now, the market appears to be treating attacks that cause no damage as background noise. A strike that disables a tanker or hits loading infrastructure near the UAE or Saudi coast would be a different matter, and would likely bring back the supply premium quickly. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: From Tokyo suburbs to the Australian outback, data centre pushback is a growing AI risk
item.description:
The backlash shifts some of the AI build-out risk from demand to delivery. Projects that are approved but slower to build stretch the gap between spending and revenue that investors are already questioning. Data centre landlords and developers with large pipelines of unapproved sites are the most exposed, while operators with powered, approved capacity could see scarcity lift rents. For Japan, a government that wants AI investment for growth now has to balance it against voters, which raises the chance of tighter zoning and slower approvals. Gas and power suppliers that have priced in data centre demand may face longer waits for that demand to arrive.

---

Earlier:

  • Australia’s AI investment ambitions hit by another data centre setback

---

Whether they're built next door or 700 km from the nearest city, data centres are finding that the hardest part of the AI boom may be getting permission.

Summary:

  • Residents near Tokyo are pushing back against data centres built close to homes, with petitions in Koto ward and a lawsuit in Inzai. Reuters reporting. 
  • Japan's government is drafting an action plan due by year-end, partly to head off disputes, as it promotes AI investment for growth
  • In Australia, a 1 GW Northern Territory project almost 700 km from the nearest city dropped its 2028 power target after the regulator paused its review
  • Local opposition blocked or delayed around 120 US projects worth nearly $200 billion in the first half of 2026, according to Data Center Watch
  • Delays push out revenue, raise costs and add risk for debt-funded projects, but can benefit operators with approved sites

Opposition to data centres is spreading from crowded suburbs to remote cattle country, and it's becoming a real constraint on the AI build-out that markets have been counting on.

Japan is the latest flashpoint. Residents living alongside a wave of new facilities around Tokyo are organising, filing petitions and, in one case, going to court, according to a Reuters report. The government, which is promoting AI investment as a driver of growth, is drafting an action plan due by year-end, partly to head off disputes.

Japan: building next door

Light regulation and political stability have made Japan a magnet for data centre investment, but about 60% of its facilities sit in and around the Tokyo area, home to about 37 million people. In Kashiwa, northeast of Tokyo, two 31-metre buildings owned by Hong Kong-based PAG now stand in front of homes, and residents complain of noise and black exhaust from monthly tests of backup generators. In Tokyo's Koto ward, a planned 51-metre facility by Singapore-based Empyrion Digital would store about 1.2 million litres of heavy oil underground, in an area rated high-risk for floods and earthquakes, less than 4 metres from an apartment block.

In Inzai, residents are suing the city and a building inspection firm. They argue that a project by Britain's Colt Data Centre Services was wrongly approved as an office rather than a factory or warehouse. Campaigners say the case could set a precedent for a zoning loophole used across the country.

Remote is no refuge

Moving away from people doesn't solve the problem. In Australia's Northern Territory, Project Ares is a planned 1 GW campus on a cattle station almost 700 km from the nearest city. It has dropped its 2028 first-power target after the territory's environmental regulator paused its assessment. The regulator flagged 10 potential impacts, including strain on water supplies and disruption to Aboriginal sacred sites, and said it had low confidence in the proposed safeguards. Closer to the cities, Goodman withdrew a Sydney project after resident opposition.

The United States shows how large the trend has become. Local opposition blocked or delayed around 120 projects worth nearly $200 billion in the first half of 2026, according to the research group Data Center Watch, which counts 843 opposition groups across 49 states.

What it means for markets

For investors, the issue is timing and cost rather than demand. Delays push out revenue for developers and data centre landlords, and they lift costs as projects add community spending, stricter safety measures or new sites. That matters most for companies whose valuations assume fast AI-driven growth.

The effect spreads further down the chain. Power and gas suppliers counting on data centre demand, equipment makers and the chipmakers whose orders depend on new capacity all face a slower and less predictable build schedule. It also adds to this week's credit worries, because projects funded with debt carry more risk when approval dates slip.

There is a flip side. Operators that already have approved, powered sites gain scarcity value, which could support their pricing power. For Japan, the outcome of the Inzai case and the government's action plan will show whether tighter rules slow a market that JLL expects to grow from about $23 billion in 2024 to about $33 billion by 2030. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Michael Burry closes his Nasdaq bets and shifts to value, but still plans an Nvidia short
item.description:
Burry's moves are small in market terms, but they are closely watched by retail traders and can shape sentiment more than their size would suggest. Closing broad index shorts after a correction removes one well-known bearish voice from the tech trade, which may encourage dip-buyers in the near term. His $200 level for a fresh Nvidia short gives traders a reference point well above current prices, which suggests he expects any rebound to be overdone before he acts. Palantir remains the clearest single-stock target of his bearish view.

---

--- Michael Burry has taken his profits on the tech selloff and moved into cash and value stocks, but his doubts about Nvidia are only on hold until the price is right.

Summary:

  • Michael Burry sold his remaining Nasdaq-100 put options as tech shares weakened, according to his Substack post on Wednesday
  • He holds about 25% cash and favors undervalued stocks, with top holdings including MercadoLibre, JD.com and Temple & Webster
  • His only remaining bearish options are on Palantir and MetLife
  • He cut his Nvidia puts by about three-quarters and bought long-dated calls, which he said have doubled since Nvidia's 31% jump on Monday
  • Burry plans to short Nvidia again nearer $200 a share during a period of market optimism
  • His positions are self-disclosed on Substack, since he closed his hedge fund last year

Michael Burry, the investor best known for betting against US housing before the 2008 crisis, has stepped back from his broad bearish bet on technology stocks. He has made clear, though, that his doubts about Nvidia haven't gone away.

In a post on his Substack on Wednesday, Burry said he had sold the remaining half of his put options on the Nasdaq-100 as technology shares weakened. Those options pay off if the tech-heavy index falls. He said he now holds about a quarter of his portfolio in cash and favors undervalued stocks. His largest holdings include Latin American e-commerce group MercadoLibre, Chinese retailer JD.com and Australian online furniture seller Temple & Webster. His only remaining bearish options positions are against Palantir and insurer MetLife.

The shift follows a series of moves on Nvidia. Burry cut his put options on the chipmaker by about three-quarters, taking profits on part of the position on Friday as tech stocks slid. He also bought a small amount of long-dated call options, which gain if the stock rises, shortly before Nvidia jumped 31% on Monday after Jensen Huang was reinstated as chief executive. He said those calls had already doubled in value.

His own comments suggest the calls were a hedge rather than a change of heart. Burry wrote that he plans to short Nvidia again nearer $200 a share during a period of market optimism, and he warned against reading the recent rebound as an all-clear for the stock.

The distinction matters for investors who follow his moves. Closing a profitable trade after a sharp fall isn't the same as abandoning the view behind it. Burry has banked gains from this month's tech selloff and kept cash ready to use, while leaving his bearish case on Nvidia intact until he gets a better price.

The way he discloses his positions has also changed. Burry closed his hedge fund, Scion Asset Management, last year and now shares his trades on Substack rather than through regulatory filings, so his positions can't be independently checked. His earlier bets against AI stocks have had mixed results: his Palantir puts performed well, while his Nvidia bets struggled for much of the year.

Taken together, the move fits a broader shift in sentiment after the correction. Bank of America this week described the selloff as a better entry point for investors. Burry's preference for undervalued stocks over broad short bets points in a similar direction, even if he remains firmly skeptical about the AI leader.

item.title: BofA sees S&P 500 at 7,800 by end-2027, a target that only takes it back to October
item.description:
A low target from a big bank rarely moves the index on its own, but it adds weight to the view that the post-correction rebound will be harder work than the consensus near 8,500 assumes. The supply-and-demand argument is worth watching: if share issuance and IPOs keep rising while buybacks slow, mega-cap tech names that rely on steady buyback demand could lag the broader market. The sector picks point to banks and health care as relative winners if 2027 turns choppy, with consumer staples likely to lag. With Thanksgiving thinning out trade, outlooks like this are likely to shape positioning more than price action this week.

---

Bank of America's 2027 target looks like an 8% gain but is really a round trip, and the bank expects even that to be bumpy.

Summary:

  • Bank of America's Savita Subramanian forecasts the S&P 500 at 7,800 by the end of 2027, about 8% above Tuesday's close
  • The target would only return the index to its October record. It was first set as a 12-month target in September, when it implied about 2% upside
  • Scenarios run from a bear case of 6,600 to a bull case of 8,500
  • The bank flags rising share issuance, fading buybacks, AI investment uncertainty and earnings risks
  • Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley target 8,700, Deutsche Bank 9,000 and JPMorgan 8,200
  • BofA favors communication services, financials, health care and consumer discretionary, and is cautious on consumer staples

Bank of America expects the S&P 500 to finish 2027 at 7,800. That looks modestly bullish on paper, but it would only return the index to where it stood in October.

Savita Subramanian, the bank's head of US equity strategy, said the target implies about 8% upside from Tuesday's close near 7,200, and she described this month's correction as a better entry point for investors. The index set a record close just above 7,800 in early October. A run of November shocks, including the exit and reinstatement of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, then pushed it down by more than 11%.

The level itself isn't new. Subramanian first set 7,800 as a 12-month target in September, when it implied only about 2% upside. The bigger percentage gain now reflects the market's decline rather than a more optimistic view.

That makes Bank of America the most cautious of the major Wall Street banks. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley both target 8,700 for the end of 2027, Deutsche Bank is at 9,000 and JPMorgan at 8,200. Bank of America's bull case of 8,500 only brings it close to the consensus, and its bear case is 6,600.

The reasons for the caution go beyond the familiar debate over AI valuations. Subramanian points to a worsening balance of supply and demand for stocks. Share issuance and new listings are rising, while buybacks, long a steady source of demand, are fading. She adds uncertainty over whether AI investment will pay off, along with earnings risks, and expects trading to stay choppy and 2027 to be a more challenging year.

The supply argument links to a theme running through markets this week. Companies building out AI are raising large amounts of money through bonds and loans. Bank of America's view suggests stock markets may face a similar strain as more shares are issued to fund growth.

The bank's sector preferences reflect that caution. It favors communication services, financials, health care and consumer discretionary, and it remains cautious on consumer staples.

For investors, the forecast is less a call for a rally than a reminder that the S&P 500 needs to recover its lost ground before it can make new progress. Bank of America sees buying opportunities after the correction, but its outlook suggests next year will reward careful stock and sector selection more than simply buying the index. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: AI's debt binge is becoming a bond market problem, South Africa's central bank warns
item.description:
The SARB's warning adds an official voice to a concern that has mostly lived in credit markets until now, and it widens the debate from tech valuations to the cost of government borrowing. The most exposed markets are emerging-market bonds and currencies, which tend to suffer first when global investors cut risk. For equities, the concentration figure is the warning sign: when so much fund exposure sits in a handful of mega-cap names, a selloff in those stocks spreads quickly through portfolios worldwide. Long-end yields and credit spreads on heavily indebted AI borrowers are the gauges to watch alongside the chip stocks.

---

Earlier:

  • A junk-rated borrower with an AA-rated customer: CoreWeave's next loan leans on Meta

---

The SARB has put into words what credit markets have been signalling all week: the AI boom's borrowing bill is now everyone's problem, governments included.

Summary:

  • The South African Reserve Bank says AI companies now compete with governments for long-term funding, adding to pressure on borrowing costs
  • The warning came in its twice-yearly Financial Stability Review, published on Wednesday
  • South African pooled funds held nearly 13% of assets in AI-related companies by the third quarter, with more than two-thirds in five big US tech stocks, including Nvidia and Microsoft
  • The bank warns disappointing AI returns could trigger a sharp tech selloff, capital outflows and tighter financial conditions, especially in emerging markets
  • It said South Africa's financial system remains resilient, with banks well capitalised and liquid
  • The warning follows record moves in CoreWeave and Nvidia credit-risk gauges this week

The borrowing behind the artificial intelligence build-out is starting to matter for bond markets as well as stocks, according to South Africa's central bank. AI companies now compete with governments for long-term funding, Governor Lesetja Kganyago said on Wednesday, and that competition is adding to pressure on long-term borrowing costs.

The warning came in the South African Reserve Bank's twice-yearly Financial Stability Review. It lands in a week when the cost of financing AI has been tested across several markets.

What the SARB found

The central bank said heavy debt issuance by AI firms is competing with sovereign borrowing, which could push up yields on South Africa's own government debt. It also flagged growing exposure at home. Local pooled investment funds held nearly 13% of their portfolio assets in AI-related companies by the third quarter, and more than two-thirds of that sat in five large US technology stocks, including Nvidia and Microsoft.

The risk, in the bank's view, is that AI investment returns disappoint. That could trigger a sharp technology selloff, capital outflows and tighter financial conditions, with emerging markets particularly exposed. The review stressed that South Africa's financial system remains resilient, with banks well capitalised and liquid, so this is a risk to watch rather than a warning of imminent stress.

A week of evidence

Recent days offer a live example of the pressures the SARB described. The cost of insuring CoreWeave's debt against default jumped by a record amount on Wednesday, and its banks are lining up a $4.5 billion loan that relies on Meta's credit rather than CoreWeave's own. Gauges of Nvidia's credit risk also hit record highs, even as Moody's kept the chipmaker's Aa1 rating, citing its exceptionally strong financial position.

That contrast is the key point. The strongest AI companies can still borrow cheaply, while the more heavily indebted operators are paying much more. The SARB's concern is the combined weight of all that borrowing on the supply of long-term capital.

Why it matters beyond South Africa

The SARB's specific warning concerned its own bond market, but the mechanism isn't unique to South Africa. Large AI borrowers draw on the same pool of long-term investors that governments rely on. With the Federal Reserve still on a hiking path, that money isn't getting any cheaper. Emerging-market governments, which typically pay more to borrow and depend more on foreign money, would likely be among the first to feel any squeeze.

For investors, the practical takeaway is that AI spending is no longer only an equity story. Credit spreads, government bond yields and capital flows into emerging markets are now worth watching alongside chip stocks.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Moody's keeps Nvidia at Aa1 after Huang's return but flags key-person and governance risks
item.description:
An unchanged rating removes one possible source of pressure on Nvidia's bonds, but it is unlikely to calm credit markets on its own, because the wider worry is leverage across the AI build-out rather than at Nvidia. For equity investors, the key-person warning is the part that sticks: the stock's reaction to Huang's exit and return showed that leadership risk is now part of its valuation. Any detail on the export-control rules Moody's referred to could matter more for Nvidia's shares than the rating itself. With US markets shut for Thanksgiving, the first proper reaction comes in Friday's shortened session.

---

  • A junk-rated borrower with an AA-rated customer: CoreWeave's next loan leans on Meta

---

Moody's is comfortable with Nvidia's balance sheet, but less so with how much the company depends on one man and the scrutiny surrounding him.

Summary:

  • Moody's kept Nvidia's Aa1 rating and stable outlook unchanged after Jensen Huang's reinstatement as chief executive
  • The agency said Huang's return restores strategic continuity but leaves some governance questions unresolved
  • It cited Nvidia's exceptionally strong competitive and financial position as the basis for the rating
  • Moody's flagged key-person risk and elevated regulatory and governmental scrutiny that could distract management
  • The rating also considers the potential impact of new export-control rules on advanced semiconductor sales
  • Huang resigned on November 12 and was reinstated by a unanimous board vote on November 23

Moody's has left Nvidia's Aa1 credit rating and stable outlook unchanged, saying Jensen Huang's return as chief executive restores strategic continuity at the AI chip leader. The agency also warned that the episode leaves some governance questions unresolved.

In comments released on Wednesday, Moody's said the rating reflects Nvidia's exceptionally strong competitive and financial position. Aa1 is Moody's second-highest grade, one notch below the top Aaa rating, so the decision confirms the agency sees no threat to Nvidia's ability to service its debt.

The caveats matter more for investors than the headline decision. Moody's said Nvidia remains exposed to key-person risk, given how much the company depends on Huang's leadership, and pointed to broader governance concerns. It said regulatory and governmental scrutiny of the company remains elevated and could take management's attention away from running the business. The agency added that its assessment also takes into account the potential impact of new export-control rules on sales of advanced semiconductors.

The review follows a turbulent fortnight. Huang resigned on November 12 after revelations about his personal conduct, including a relationship with a woman US intelligence reportedly believes to be a Chinese spy. Chief financial officer Colette Kress became interim chief executive, and the board appointed its first-ever chair. On November 23, the board voted unanimously to reinstate Huang. It said it was satisfied with his candor and had received input from senior levels of the US government indicating his return posed no national security risk. Investigations into the company's conduct are continuing.

For markets, the Moody's view helps separate two different worries. Huang's resignation contributed to a sharp selloff in US stocks, and his reinstatement sparked a strong rebound. That showed how much of the AI trade rests on a single company and, in turn, a single executive. Credit markets remain uneasy about AI more broadly, though. Gauges of Nvidia's own credit risk hit record highs this week, alongside sharper stress at heavily indebted AI operators such as CoreWeave.

Moody's assessment suggests that pressure reflects sector-wide nerves about borrowing and spending rather than any weakness in Nvidia's balance sheet. The risks it highlighted, from export controls to regulatory scrutiny and succession, are the ones to watch. They could affect Nvidia's earnings power long before they threaten its credit quality.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold claws back $160 from a 14-month low, but one candle doesn't necessarily make a bottom
item.description:
Reclaiming $3,500 gives gold bulls a floor to defend, but there's little sign of a confirmed turn until prices clear last week's high near $3,900. Silver followed the same path, bouncing from below $38 to above $41, which suggests broad short covering across precious metals rather than buying driven by gold alone. With US markets closed for Thanksgiving and Friday a short session, thin liquidity could exaggerate the next move in either direction. The bigger test comes with the Fed's December 9 decision, when the bank's guidance on further hikes is likely to matter more for real yields, and for gold, than the hike itself.

---

Earlier:

  • Gold bulls may have been waiting months for a chart like this

---

Gold found buyers at its lowest level since September 2025, but bank forecasts ranging from $3,340 to $5,000 show how little agreement there is on where this correction ends.

Summary:

  • Gold fell to around $3,425 on Wednesday, its lowest since September 2025, after hot US core PCE inflation and strong GDP data
  • It then rebounded about $160 to close near $3,590, up almost 1% on the day
  • Lower Treasury yields, a softer dollar and a recovery in US stocks, which eased margin-driven selling, supported the reversal
  • Natixis analyst Bernard Dahdah sees a risk of $3,340 by January as central bank buying slows
  • UBS forecasts $5,000 by end-2027, with Goldman Sachs at $4,650, JPMorgan at $4,500 and Commerzbank at $4,100
  • Gold remains roughly a third below its January record close

Gold made a sharp turnaround on Wednesday, recovering about $160 from a 14-month low to close near the top of its range. It did so even as US data gave the Federal Reserve more reason to keep raising rates.

The metal fell to around $3,425 an ounce after the October PCE report, its weakest level since September 2025. That broke the $3,500 support that had held through last week's rout. Core PCE inflation, the Fed's preferred gauge, rose to 3.3% from 3.1%, and third-quarter GDP growth came in at 4.3%, well ahead of expectations. Buyers then stepped in, and gold finished near $3,590, up almost 1% on the day.

The rebound came from the bond and currency markets rather than from any rush to safety. Treasury yields fell after the data and the dollar slipped, while pricing for a December Fed hike eased slightly from near-certain levels. Wall Street also recovered, with the Dow erasing a deep intraday loss to close higher. That eased the margin-driven selling that had forced some investors to sell gold to raise cash during last week's slide of roughly 9%.

Whether Wednesday marks a bottom is another matter. Natixis precious metals analyst Bernard Dahdah expects gold could fall to $3,340 by January. His stress test assumes central bank buying drops a quarter below 2025 levels, and he sees signs that the official-sector demand behind the rally is fading. He points to Poland, whose central bank has reached its 700-tonne reserve target, and argues that most of the accumulation is likely done. Higher rates, a stronger dollar and softer investment demand complete his bearish case.

Other banks see the selloff as a reset rather than the end of the bull market. UBS forecasts gold at $5,000 by the end of 2027 and still rates the metal Attractive, citing central bank diversification, rising sovereign debt and Chinese demand. Goldman Sachs expects $4,650 over the same period, JPMorgan $4,500 and Commerzbank $4,100.

Even after Wednesday's bounce, gold is still roughly a third below its January record close above $5,400. The Fed decides on December 9, and a hike that month is still close to fully priced. One strong candle may be the start of a base, but it doesn't necessarily make a bottom.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: A junk-rated borrower with an AA-rated customer: CoreWeave's next loan leans on Meta
item.description:
Credit markets are moving ahead of equities on AI risk, and that is the main warning sign for the Nasdaq and the wider tech-heavy indices. If borrowing costs keep rising for the most heavily indebted AI operators, chipmakers and cloud names could come under pressure next, since their growth depends on that spending continuing. Meta looks the safer side of the trade for now, because lenders are treating its contracts as close to bankable. With Wall Street shut for Thanksgiving, Asian tech stocks and Japanese banks such as MUFG may carry the first reaction in thin trade.

---

Earlier:

  • U.S. stocks close mixed as Dow reverses a 1,105-point drop

---

CoreWeave can still borrow cheaply, but only by using Meta's credit, and that says a lot about how bond investors now see the AI build-out.

Summary:

  • Morgan Stanley and MUFG are preparing to sell a loan of up to $4.5 billion for CoreWeave as soon as next week, according to Bloomberg
  • The loan is tied to Meta's contract with CoreWeave, worth $14.2 billion through 2031, and is expected to get investment-grade ratings
  • Early pricing talk puts the loan yield at around 7% to 7.5%, against roughly 18% on CoreWeave's existing junk-rated bonds
  • The cost of insuring CoreWeave's debt against default jumped by a record on Wednesday, implying about a 70% chance of default over five years
  • Credit-risk gauges for Nvidia, Oracle and Alphabet also hit records, adding to worries about tech-sector borrowing

Banks for CoreWeave are preparing to sell a loan of up to $4.5 billion as soon as next week, Bloomberg reported. The deal will show whether investors are still willing to fund the AI build-out at a time when worries about the debt behind it have hit new highs.

Morgan Stanley and MUFG are arranging the financing, and what matters most is whose credit stands behind it. CoreWeave rents out Nvidia-powered computing capacity to large technology customers and has a junk credit rating. The new loan, however, is tied to its contract with Meta Platforms, which has committed $14.2 billion to CoreWeave's cloud services through 2031. That link is expected to earn the loan investment-grade ratings, with early talk of a yield around 7% to 7.5%. CoreWeave's existing bonds yield about 18%, which shows how differently lenders view the company and its biggest customer.

The timing is difficult. The cost of insuring CoreWeave's debt against default rose by a record amount on Wednesday, according to ICE Data Services figures reported by Bloomberg. Credit default swaps now imply roughly a 70% chance of default over five years. CoreWeave's total debt is now above $46 billion.

The stress is spreading beyond one company. Credit-risk gauges for Nvidia, Oracle and Alphabet also hit records this week, a sign that bond investors are uneasy about how much the tech sector is borrowing to pay for data centers and chips. Banks have also been pulling back from lending to AI data centers in Asia.

For stock markets, this matters because AI spending has been a major driver of gains in the Nasdaq and the S&P 500. If heavily indebted operators find credit harder to get, the spending that supports chipmakers and cloud providers could slow, and that would hit the market's biggest names.

Meta's position is different. The loan works because lenders trust Meta to pay, which shows how much the AI ecosystem depends on a small group of cash-rich giants.

With US markets closed for Thanksgiving and Friday a shortened session, the real answer comes next week. A smooth sale at investment-grade pricing would ease some nerves. A struggle to place it would suggest the credit market is losing patience with AI borrowing.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold bulls may have been waiting months for a chart like this
item.description:
Gold futures: A potential turning point at the intersection of two major price channels

The daily gold futures chart shows an interesting convergence of three technical references, following a substantial decline from the record high of $5,626.80.

The zoomed-out chart: Gold has been trading within a broad ascending channel spanning several years. Since reaching its record high in early 2026, however, gold has developed a descending channel within that much larger bullish structure.

The latest selloff has brought gold to the lower boundaries of both channels, creating an area of potential technical support.

The zoomed-in chart: Gold futures briefly broke below both channel boundaries and the horizontal price reference at $3,433.18, reaching a low of $3,425.20 before recovering to $3,571.70 at the time of the chart snapshot.

That represents a rebound of approximately 4.28% from the session low, leaving a prominent lower wick on the developing daily candle.

Why this may be significant for gold traders and investors

There are three elements worth considering:

  • Long-term support: The lower boundary of a multiyear ascending channel is being tested, putting the broader bullish structure under scrutiny.

  • Potential downside exhaustion: Gold has also tested and recovered above the lower boundary of its 2026 descending channel.

  • Possible failed breakdown: The recovery above $3,433.18 and both trendlines suggests that sellers have, so far, struggled to sustain prices below these technical references.

The convergence of these three elements is more interesting than a test of an isolated trendline or horizontal support level.

What gold bulls need to see next

The developing daily candle is encouraging for gold bulls, but its closing price and the market's behavior over the next few sessions could be more revealing.

Sustained trading above both channel boundaries would strengthen the case for a meaningful recovery. Conversely, renewed selling and sustained acceptance below $3,425.20 would weaken that interpretation and raise concerns about the integrity of the multiyear ascending channel.

For longer-term gold investors, this is an area worth monitoring for potential accumulation opportunities. For active traders, the immediate question is whether the sharp rejection of lower prices develops into a more sustainable reversal.

Gold does not need to end its 2026 downtrend for a substantial recovery to take place. Even a rebound within the descending channel could present opportunities.

The chart offers a compelling location to investigate a potential bottom, not confirmation that one has already been established.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Economic and event calendar in Asia Thursday, November 26, 2026: BoK, BoJ, turkey later
item.description:
Bank of Korea: another hike looks likely

The Bank of Korea announces its last policy decision of 2026 at around 0100 GMT (2000 US Eastern on Wednesday), and markets expect a rate rise. A Reuters poll published on November 24 found 32 of 34 economists expect a 25 basis point increase to 3.25%. That would follow hikes in July and August and a pause at 3% in October. Strong semiconductor-led exports, inflation above the 2% target and rising home prices make the case for tightening. The board also releases updated economic projections. For the won, Governor Rhee Chang-yong's guidance matters as much as the hike itself. Economists in the same poll see a final hike to 3.50% early next year.

BoJ's Tamura: a hawk speaks before December

BoJ board member Naoki Tamura speaks to local leaders in Yamanashi at 1000 JST (0100 GMT, 2000 US Eastern on Wednesday). Tamura is firmly in the hawkish camp. He has argued the neutral rate is likely near 2% and called for steady rate increases, which leaves plenty of room above the current 1.25% policy rate. A December hike is already the base case: 61 of 71 economists in a Reuters poll expect a move to 1.5% at the December 17-18 meeting. Markets care less about December than about what comes after it. Any comments from Tamura on how fast and how far rates should rise are the ones to watch for the yen.

US Thanksgiving: Wall Street shut, Asia set to drift

US stock markets are closed today for Thanksgiving, and SIFMA recommends a full close for US bond markets.

Without a US, Asian trade is likely to thin out, and traders may hold back from new positions with liquidity light for the rest of the week. Thin markets can still move sharply, though, and an unexpected headline from Seoul or Tamura could get an outsized reaction.

Friday is a short session. The NYSE and Nasdaq close at 1:00 p.m. US Eastern (1800 GMT), and SIFMA recommends that bonds close at 2:00 p.m. (1900 GMT).

item.title: Beige Book: Eight of 12 districts report growth as wage pressures pick up
item.description:
• Eight districts reported growth in the slight to moderate range, and four reported no change. In October, nine grew and three were unchanged.
  • Consumer spending was little changed as households remained price sensitive and selective.
  • Employment rose slightly on balance, with hiring mostly to replace attrition.
  • Wages and benefits rose moderately, up from modest in the prior report.
  • Prices increased moderately overall, as in the prior period.
  • Input cost growth generally outpaced increases in selling prices.
  • Most districts expect slight to moderate growth.

The November Beige Book shows an economy grinding sideways rather than deteriorating further, but the inflation story has shifted from prices to wages. Boston slipped to no change from slight growth, joining Chicago, Kansas City and San Francisco in the flat column. Dallas slowed to modest from moderate. Cleveland was the lone upgrade, to moderate growth, on robust manufacturing demand tied to data centers, power generation and defense. Construction declined amid higher borrowing and building costs, and residential real estate weakened.

Wages are the most important change. Wages and benefits rose moderately after modest gains in October, with pressure concentrated in hard-to-fill roles and driven by cost-of-living demands and rising benefit costs. Philadelphia said wage inflation has reached a moderate pace for the first time since 2023, and its contacts expect wage and benefit increases next year at rates last seen in 2023. Dallas reported service-sector wage growth accelerating to an above-average pace. Minneapolis contacts said wages "will certainly have to follow" prices.

On prices, the tone was calmer than October. The national summary no longer tallies robust districts or flags accelerating ones; it simply says prices rose moderately, as before. New York said selling price increases eased slightly, and Minneapolis noted a smaller share of firms reporting higher input costs as fuel prices eased. The pipeline is still full, though. Cleveland reported robust nonlabor cost pressures for a 12th straight period, with one manufacturer planning a 19% contract price increase at the start of the year. Richmond manufacturers' price growth topped 5% for the first time since 2023. St. Louis said many recent cost increases won't hit customers until next quarter. Consumer-facing firms still can't pass costs through, so margins are taking the hit.

The consumer is holding up in aggregate but fraying underneath. Kansas City said spending rose modestly after three straight months of declines, but it also reported workers using earned wage access to pay for workplace meals and households hitting their financial limits on unexpected repairs. Philadelphia retailers saw a late-October lift as gas prices eased and the midterms were resolved, while credit card volumes unusually fell heading into the holidays. Cleveland said food and housing insecurity now reaches middle- to upper-income county employees.

Higher rates are a bigger theme than last time. Dallas cited mortgage rates eclipsing 7%, and its bankers warned that further rate hikes could hurt borrowers' ability to repay. Cleveland bankers said commercial clients are rushing to lock in rates ahead of anticipated increases.

This report is less stagflationary on the price side than October's, but the wage pickup is exactly what the Fed doesn't want to see with inflation already elevated. The FOMC meets Dec. 8-9 and the market is almost fully priced for a hike.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.
